explanation.text:
(Pro. 17:1-28)

sacrifices--or, "feasts" made with part of them (compare Pro 7:14; Lev 2:3; Lev 7:31).

with--literally, "of."

strife--its product, or attendant.

bsb.text: Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife.

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 14:35).

causeth shame-- (Pro 10:5).

shall . . . inheritance--that is, share a brother's part (compare Num 27:4, Num 27:7).

bsb.text: A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son and share his inheritance as one of the brothers.

explanation.text: God only knows, as He tries (Psa 12:6; Psa 66:10) the heart.

bsb.text: A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts.

explanation.text: Wicked doers and speakers alike delight in calumny.

bsb.text: A wicked man listens to evil lips; a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue.

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 14:31).

glad at calamities--rejoicing in others' evil. Such are rightly punished by God, who knows their hearts.

bsb.text: He who mocks the poor insults their Maker; whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished.

explanation.text: Prolonged posterity is a blessing, its cutting off a curse (Pro 13:22; Psa 109:13-15), hence children may glory in virtuous ancestry.

bsb.text: Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of a son is his father.

explanation.text: Excellent speech--(Compare Margin). Such language as ill suits a fool, as lying (ought to suit) a prince (Pro 16:12-13).

bsb.text: Eloquent words are unfit for a fool; how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!

explanation.text: One so corrupt as to take a bribe evinces his high estimate of it by subjection to its influence (Pro 18:16; Pro 19:6).

bsb.text: A bribe is a charm to its giver; wherever he turns, he succeeds.

explanation.text: seeketh love--(Compare Margin). The contrast is between the peace-maker and tale-bearer.

bsb.text: Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends.

explanation.text: Reproof more affects the wise than severe scourging, fools.

bsb.text: A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool.

explanation.text:
Such meet just retribution (Kg1 2:25).

a cruel messenger--one to inflict it.

bsb.text: An evil man seeks only rebellion; a cruel messenger will be sent against him.

explanation.text: They are less rational in anger than wild beasts.

bsb.text: It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly.

explanation.text:
(Compare Psa 7:4; Psa 35:12).

evil--injury to another (Pro 13:21).

bsb.text: If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house.

explanation.text:
letteth . . . water--as a breach in a dam.

before . . . meddled with--before strife has become sharp, or, by an explanation better suiting the figure, before it rolls on, or increases.

bsb.text: To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out.

explanation.text: abomination . . . Lord--as reversing His method of acting (Pro 3:32; Pro 12:2).

bsb.text: Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD.

explanation.text: Though wealth cannot buy wisdom for those who do not love it, yet wisdom procures wealth (Pro 3:16; Pro 14:24).

bsb.text: Why should the fool have money in his hand with no intention of buying wisdom?

explanation.text: To the second of these parallel clauses, there is an accession of meaning, that is, that a brother's love is specially seen in adversity.

bsb.text: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 6:1-5; Pro 11:15).

in the presence, etc.--that is, he either fails to consult his friend, or to follow his advice.

bsb.text: A man lacking judgment strikes hands in pledge and puts up security for his neighbor.

explanation.text:
strife--contention is, and leads to, sin.

he that exalteth his gate--gratifies a vain love of costly building.

seeketh--or, "findeth," as if he sought (compare "loveth death," Pro 8:36).

bsb.text: He who loves transgression loves strife; he who builds his gate high invites destruction.

explanation.text: The second clause advances on the first. The ill-natured fail of good, and the cavilling and fault-finding incur evil.

bsb.text: The one with a perverse heart finds no good, and he whose tongue is deceitful falls into trouble.

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 23:24). Different words are rendered by "fool," both denoting stupidity and impiety.

bsb.text: A man fathers a fool to his own grief; the father of a fool has no joy.

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 14:30; Pro 15:13). The effect of the mind on the body is well known.

medicine--or, "body," which better corresponds with "bone."

drieth--as if the marrow were exhausted.

bsb.text: A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones.

explanation.text:
a gift . . . bosom--Money and other valuables were borne in a fold of the garment, called the bosom.

to pervert--that is, by bribery.

bsb.text: A wicked man takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice.

explanation.text: Wisdom . . . him--ever an object of regard, while a fool's affections are unsettled.

bsb.text: Wisdom is the focus of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth.

explanation.text: a grief--or cross, vexation (compare Pro 17:21; Pro 10:1).

bsb.text: A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.

explanation.text: Also--that is, Equally to be avoided are other sins: punishing good subjects, or resisting good rulers.

bsb.text: It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty.

explanation.text:
Prudence of speech is commended as is an excellent or calm spirit, not excited to vain conversation.

bsb.text: A man of knowledge restrains his words, and a man of understanding maintains a calm spirit.

explanation.text:
Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise,.... Not only one that is sparing of his words, and is really a man of knowledge and understanding; but even a feel, if he is but silent, and does not betray his folly by his words, will be reckoned a wise man by those that do not know him; and, whatever fool he may be in other respects, yet in this he acts the wise part, that he holds his peace and says nothing;

and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding; and keeps them shut, lest he should say anything rashly and hastily; a man that has so much command of himself as not to speak unadvisedly, through the heat of his own passions, and through the provocations of others, will pass for a man that understands himself, and knows how to behave well before others.

bsb.text: Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue.
